reading.title: The Silent Galleries
reading.intro_zh: 这篇短文讲一个真实话题：纽约大都会艺术博物馆为什么几乎从不演奏馆藏的古乐器，以及它如何在“保存”与“被听见”之间取舍。改编自史密森尼杂志（Smithsonian Magazine）对大都会博物馆乐器录音项目的报道。

source.title: Now Streaming, the Swan Songs of the Met's Historic Instruments

passage: Step into the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and you will move past glass cases crowded with antique violins, harps, and keyboards, yet the rooms themselves stay strangely hushed. The museum keeps about five thousand musical instruments, but only a tiny fraction are ever kept ready to play. The silence is not the product of neglect; it is a deliberate choice. Many of these objects were built from perishable materials such as animal skin, slender plant fibre, and timber that has dried and weakened with age, so the strain of being struck, bowed, or blown can split a panel or break a string that has lasted for hundreds of years. Because such damage usually cannot be undone, curators treat each performance as a measured gamble rather than an everyday liberty.

Before a single note sounds, the conservation staff balance the insight that playing might reveal against the harm it could cause. When an instrument is found robust enough, the museum invites only a specialist who truly grasps how it behaves, and the whole session is carefully recorded. This care reflects a deeper tension in the field: an instrument that is never played falls mute and its character slowly fades from memory, while one that is played too often wears itself away. To sidestep that trap, the Met has produced high-quality recordings of around forty selected instruments, so visitors can call up their sound through gallery kiosks or their own phones. The delicate originals remain safe behind glass, while their voices live on in a form that no clumsy touch can spoil.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The Met wants to sell its musical instruments to private collectors.
Antique instruments sound better than modern ones.
Museums protect fragile historic instruments by rarely playing them and recording them instead.
Visitors are forbidden from entering the instrument galleries.
questions.explanation_zh: 全文的核心是：博物馆为了保护脆弱的古乐器，几乎不演奏它们，而是用高质量录音让公众听到它们的声音。

questions.question: According to the passage, how many of the Met's instruments are kept ready to play?
options: Only a small fraction of them.
Roughly half of the five thousand.
Almost all five thousand.
None of them at all.
questions.explanation_zh: 文中说博物馆约有五千件乐器，但只有极少数（a tiny fraction）被保持在可演奏状态。

questions.question: Why does playing many of these instruments pose such a serious risk?
options: The musicians are not skilled enough to handle them.
The galleries are too cold for the wood.
The instruments are kept in locked cases that are hard to open.
Their delicate materials can crack or break, and the damage usually cannot be undone.
questions.explanation_zh: 文中说乐器由动物皮、纤细植物纤维和老化木材等易损材料制成，演奏带来的应力可能使其开裂或断弦，而这种损坏通常无法挽回。

questions.question: What can we infer about why the Met makes recordings of its instruments?
options: It wants people to hear the instruments without endangering the fragile originals.
It no longer cares whether the instruments survive.
Recordings sound exactly like a live concert in every way.
It plans to stop displaying the instruments to the public.
questions.explanation_zh: 可以推断：录音让公众能听到乐器的声音，同时避免反复演奏对脆弱原件造成伤害——这正是为了在保存与被听见之间取得平衡。

questions.question: In the passage, the phrase "cannot be undone" most nearly means
options: easily repeated many times.
impossible to reverse or repair.
extremely expensive to clean.
surprising but harmless.
questions.explanation_zh: “cannot be undone”意为“无法逆转、不可挽回”；文中指乐器一旦受损往往无法修复，所以演奏被视为有风险的行为。

writing.intro_zh: 今天的句式仿写把被动语态当成“物品的一生”来写：它叫什么、在哪里制造、属于谁多久、被谁损坏，以及问题之后的新规则。请把句子写得更长、更抽象，尽量描述博物馆藏品、传家旧物或珍贵器物等更正式的语境。

patterns.title: It is called ...
patterns.focus_zh: 用 It is called 给一个物品命名，适合介绍学生不熟悉的旧物或工具。
patterns.task_zh: 仿写一句：为一件博物馆藏品或珍贵旧物命名，并补充一个说明它身份或特点的从句。
patterns.sample: It is called a clavichord, an early keyboard instrument far more fragile than any modern piano.
patterns.tip_zh: called 后面直接接名字或类别，不要再加 as。

patterns.title: was made in ...
patterns.source: It was made in Germany in 1681.
patterns.focus_zh: 用 was made in 交代一个物品的产地、年代或制作地点，让它有历史感。
patterns.task_zh: 仿写一句：说明一件历史器物在何地、何时被制造，并暗示它惊人的年代或工艺。
patterns.sample: The delicate ivory keyboard was made in a Florentine workshop in 1681, long before the modern piano existed.
patterns.tip_zh: was made in 后面可以接地点，也可以再接年份。

patterns.title: has belonged to ... for ...
patterns.source: It has belonged to our family for a long time.
patterns.focus_zh: 用 has belonged to ... for ... 表示从过去到现在一直属于某人或某个地方。
patterns.task_zh: 仿写一句：说明一件珍贵器物已经长期属于某个机构或家族，并补充它经历过什么。
patterns.sample: This battered violin has belonged to the museum's collection for more than a century, surviving wars and countless moves.
patterns.tip_zh: belong to 后面接拥有者；for 后面接持续的时间。

patterns.title: was damaged by ...
patterns.source: Recently it was damaged by a visitor.
patterns.focus_zh: 用 was damaged by 写“东西受损”这件事，重点放在物品上，而不是先指责某个人。
patterns.task_zh: 仿写一句：用被动语态描述一件器物如何被某次动作或事故损坏，并说明后果可能无法挽回。
patterns.sample: The centuries-old harp was damaged by a single careless performance, and the cracked soundboard may never be fully restored.
patterns.tip_zh: by 后面写造成损坏的人或原因；语气可以客观，不必骂人。

patterns.title: are not allowed to ...
patterns.source: Now we are not allowed to touch it.
patterns.focus_zh: 用 are not allowed to 写问题之后的新规则，表达“不是不能欣赏，而是不能随便碰”。
patterns.task_zh: 仿写一句：写一条保护脆弱器物的正式规则，并说明设立这条规则的原因。
patterns.sample: Because the originals are so fragile, ordinary visitors are not allowed to touch the instruments without a trained conservator present.
patterns.tip_zh: are not allowed to 后面接动词原形，适合写清楚边界。
